messages.content: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: You are working on Campfire, a Rails chat application. Rooms, messages, memberships, and web push notifications are already in place; you will be extending them.

Feel free to store any design notes/insights that could be useful for future steps in the docs/ folder.

Follow the codebase conventions.

Our QA auto-tests drive the app in a browser and rely on the labels in quotes in each task. Keep them exactly as written, as visible text, a <label>, a placeholder, or an aria-label.

The QA auto-tests also expect:

- Switches are checkboxes (a styled switch is fine if a real checkbox sits under it).
- Confirmations use the browser's native `confirm()` dialog.

Some bots misbehave: they flood rooms, or their webhooks keep failing.

> As an administrator, I want misbehaving bots to be stopped automatically,
> and I want to decide when they come back.

Flooding:

- A bot may post at most 10 messages in any 10 seconds. Messages posted through the API and webhook replies both count.
- The message that goes over the limit is rejected and starts a 30-second cooldown. During the cooldown, the posting endpoint responds with `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header (seconds left), and webhook replies are not posted.
- Five more attempts to post during the same cooldown suspend the bot.

Failing webhooks:

- A failed delivery is any response other than `2xx`, a timeout, or a connection error.
- Ten failed deliveries in a row suspend the bot. A successful delivery resets the count.

A suspended bot:

- gets `403 Forbidden` from the posting endpoint;
- receives no webhooks;
- keeps its rooms and messages, and still counts towards its owner's bot limit;
- stays listed on the bots page and shows as "Suspended", with the reason.

Only administrators can reactivate a suspended bot, from the bots page: a "Reactivate" button that asks for confirmation. The limits above are fixed in code; they have no settings.

{

  "output_head": "# Bots Design Notes

## Data Model

Bots are modeled as `User` records with `role: :bot` (`enum :role, %i[ member administrator bot ]` in `User::Role`) and bot-specific behavior in `User::Bot`:

- `users.bot_token` (string, unique index): 24-character `SecureRandom.base58(24)` secret (~140 bits of entropy), generated on create via `before_validation :initialize_bot, on: :create, if: :bot?`.
- `users.creator_id` (foreign key to `users`, `on_delete: :nullify`): tracks the user who created the bot so `User#can_administer?` works uniformly for bots (creators manage their own bots; administrators manage all bots).
- `users.add_to_all_open_rooms` (boolean, default `false`, `null: false`): controls whether the bot automatically joins all open rooms (existing ones when enabled and future ones created or converted to open).
- `users.password_digest`: initialized to `""` on bot creation (`has_secure_password` returns `false` for all password checks when blank). `email_address` remains `nil`.
- `User#bot_key`: returns `"#{id}-#{bot_token}"` for active bots.

## Authentication & Authorization

- **Bot credential verification (`User.authenticate_bot`)**: splits `bot_key` into `id` and `token`, validates `id` is strictly digits (`/\A\d+\z/`), looks up `User.active.bot.find_by(id: id)`, and verifies `bot_token` with `ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare`.
- **Bot management UI (`/bots`)**:
  - Accessible to all signed-in chat members via `/account/edit` ("Set up chat bots").
  - Members see only active bots they created; administrators see all active bots. Rendered on one page without pagination.
  - `BotsController` sets `Cache-Control: no-store` on `index` and `edit` because bot codes are sensitive credentials.
  - `edit`, `update`, and `destroy` scope to `User.active.bot` (returning `404` for human users or deleted bots) and enforce `Current.user.can_administer?(@bot)` (returning `403` for other members' bots).
- **Deletion**: deleting a bot calls `User#deactivate`, which marks the bot `deactivated`, clears `bot_token` to `nil`, removes non-direct room memberships, and preserves previously posted messages with the bot shown as author. Deactivated bots immediately fail authentication with `401 Unauthorized`.
- **Human-only surfaces**: `AccountsController`, `Accounts::UsersController`, `SessionsController`, `Sessions::TransfersController`, and `Users::BansController` scope to `User.without_bots` so bots cannot log in via web sessions or transfer links, do not appear in the people list on `/account/edit`, cannot be promoted/demoted, and cannot be banned.
- **Log filtering**: `bot_token` and route param `:bot_key` match `:token` and `:_key` in `config/initializers/filter_parameter_logging.rb`, filtering them in logs and `ActiveRecord#inspect`.

## Room Membership

- Bots do **not** join open rooms by default (`users.add_to_all_open_rooms` defaults to `false`). People still automatically join all open rooms (`User#auto_joins_open_rooms?` returns `!bot? || add_to_all_open_rooms?`, and `User.auto_joining_open_rooms` matches all non-bots plus bots with `add_to_all_open_rooms: true`).
- The bot form (`/bots/new` and `/bots/:id/edit`) includes a checkbox switch labelled `"Add to all open rooms"` (off by default):
  - When created with `"Add to all open rooms"` on (`after_create_commit :grant_membership_to_open_rooms_on_create`) or toggled from off to on (`after_update_commit :grant_membership_to_open_rooms_on_update`), the bot joins all existing `Rooms::Open` it is not already in.
  - Creating or converting an open room (`Rooms::Open#grant_access_to_all_users`) grants membership to `User.active.auto_joining_open_rooms` (active people + active opt-in bots).
  - Turning `"Add to all open rooms"` off keeps all of the bot's current memberships; future open rooms simply do not auto-add it.
- Open room forms (`Rooms::OpensController#new` and `#edit`) show static checkmarks for people and opt-in bots (`auto_joins_open_rooms?`) and toggle switches (`user_ids[]`) for manual bots (`add_to_all_open_rooms: false`), allowing room admins to add or remove manual bots from individual open rooms without affecting people or opt-in bots. Non-admins viewing an open room's settings see only its actual active members.
- Closed room forms (`Rooms::ClosedsController`) and direct room / mention autocomplete (`Autocompletable::UsersController`) use `User.active` (scoped to room members for room mention autocomplete), allowing bots to be added to closed and direct rooms the same way as people.

## Bot HTTP API

- Route: `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages` (`Messages::ByBotsController#create`), with segment constraints `{ room_id: /[^\/]+/, bot_key: /[^\/]+/ }` so malformed segments (including dotted strings) still route to the controller for proper `401`/`404` handling.
- Skips web session auth, CSRF verification, and `allow_browser` checks.
- Overrides `set_request!` to short-circuit `request_parameters` parsing for non-multipart requests so ",

class Room < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :memberships, dependent: :delete_all do
    def grant_to(users)
      room = proxy_association.owner
      records = Array(users).collect { |user| { room_id: room.id, user_id: user.id, involvement: room.default_involvement } }
      Membership.grant_records(records)
    end

    def revoke_from(users)
      destroy_by user: users
    end

    def revise(granted: [], revoked: [])
      transaction do
        grant_to(granted) if granted.present?
        revoke_from(revoked) if revoked.present?
      end
    end
  end

  has_many :users, through: :memberships
  has_many :messages, dependent: :destroy

  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  validate :direct_rooms_keep_their_type, on: :update

  scope :opens,           -> { where(type: "Rooms::Open") }
  scope :closeds,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Closed") }
  scope :directs,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Direct") }
  scope :without_directs, -> { where.not(type: "Rooms::Direct") }

  scope :ordered, -> { order("LOWER(name)") }

  class << self
    def create_for(attributes, users:)
      transaction do
        create!(attributes).tap do |room|
          room.memberships.grant_to users
        end
      end
    end

    def original
      order(:created_at).first
    end
  end

  def receive(message)
    unread_memberships(message)
    push_later(message)
    deliver_webhooks_later(message)
  end

  def open?
    is_a?(Rooms::Open)
  end

  def closed?
    is_a?(Rooms::Closed)
  end

  def direct?
    is_a?(Rooms::Direct)
  end

  def default_involvement
    "mentions"
  end

  private
    # Open and closed rooms convert into each other freely. A direct room can't become
    # either: its participants agreed to a private conversation, not to one whose
    # audience someone else gets to widen afterwards.
    def direct_rooms_keep_their_type
      if type_changed? && type_was == "Rooms::Direct"
        errors.add :type, "can't be changed for a direct room"
      end
    end

    def unread_memberships(message)
      memberships.visible.disconnected.where.not(user: message.creator).update_all(unread_at: message.created_at, updated_at: Time.current)
    end

    def push_later(message)
      Room::PushMessageJob.perform_later(self, message)
    end

    def deliver_webhooks_later(message)
      message.deliver_webhooks_later
    end
end

require "test_helper"

class User::BotTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  test "creating a bot sets role, generates unique bot_token and bot_key, and does not join open rooms by default" do
    bot = nil
    assert_no_difference -> { Membership.count } do
      bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Deploy Bot", creator: users(:kevin))
    end

    assert bot.bot?
    assert bot.active?
    assert_not bot.add_to_all_open_rooms?
    assert_equal users(:kevin), bot.creator
    assert_equal "", bot.password_digest
    assert_nil bot.email_address
    assert_match /\A[A-Za-z0-9]{24}\z/, bot.bot_token
    assert_equal "#{bot.id}-#{bot.bot_token}", bot.bot_key
    assert_empty bot.rooms

    other_bot = User.create_bot!(name: "CI Bot", creator: users(:kevin))
    assert_not_equal bot.bot_token, other_bot.bot_token
    assert_not_equal bot.bot_key, other_bot.bot_key
  end

  test "creating a bot with add_to_all_open_rooms joins all existing open rooms" do
    bot = nil
    assert_difference -> { Membership.count }, +Rooms::Open.count do
      bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Everyone Bot", creator: users(:kevin), add_to_all_open_rooms: true)
    end

    assert bot.add_to_all_open_rooms?
    assert_equal Rooms::Open.pluck(:id).sort, bot.rooms.pluck(:id).sort
  end

  test "toggling add_to_all_open_rooms on joins missing open rooms and toggling off keeps current memberships" do
    bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Toggle Bot", creator: users(:kevin))
    rooms(:hq).memberships.grant_to(bot)
    rooms(:watercooler).memberships.grant_to(bot)

    assert_equal [ rooms(:hq).id, rooms(:watercooler).id ].sort, bot.rooms.pluck(:id).sort

    # Turning on adds missing open rooms without duplicating existing memberships
    assert_difference -> { Membership.count }, +(Rooms::Open.count - 1) do
      bot.update!(add_to_all_open_rooms: true)
    end
    assert_equal (Rooms::Open.pluck(:id) + [ rooms(:watercooler).id ]).sort, bot.reload.rooms.pluck(:id).sort

    # Turning off keeps all existing memberships
    assert_no_difference -> { Membership.count } do
      bot.update!(add_to_all_open_rooms: false)
    end
    assert_equal (Rooms::Open.pluck(:id) + [ rooms(:watercooler).id ]).sort, bot.reload.rooms.pluck(:id).sort

    # New open rooms created while off do not include the bot
    later_open = Rooms::Open.create!(name: "Later Open", creator: users(:david))
    assert_not_includes later_open.users, bot

    # Turning back on joins the newly created open room
    assert_difference -> { Membership.count }, +1 do
      bot.update!(add_to_all_open_rooms: true)
    end
    assert_includes later_open.reload.users, bot
  end

  test "bot name is required" do
    bot = User.new(role: :bot, name: "   ", creator: users(:kevin))
    assert_not bot.valid?
    assert_includes bot.errors[:name], "can't be blank"
  end

  test "creating and updating a bot manages its optional webhook" do
    bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Deploy Bot", creator: users(:kevin), webhook_url: "  https://bot.example.com/hook  ")
    assert_equal "https://bot.example.com/hook", bot.webhook.url
    assert_equal "https://bot.example.com/hook", bot.webhook_url

    original_webhook_id = bot.webhook.id

    # Updating name without webhook_url preserves existing webhook
    bot.update!(name: "Release Bot")
    assert_equal original_webhook_id, bot.reload.webhook.id
    assert_equal "https://bot.example.com/hook", bot.webhook_url

    # Updating webhook_url updates existing webhook in place
    bot.update!(webhook_url: "http://127.0.0.1:4567/events")
    assert_equal original_webhook_id, bot.reload.webhook.id
    assert_equal "http://127.0.0.1:4567/events", bot.webhook_url

    # Invalid update on name does not delete existing webhook
    assert_not bot.update(name: "", webhook_url: "")
    assert_equal "http://127.0.0.1:4567/events", bot.reload.webhook.url
    assert_equal "http://127.0.0.1:4567/events", bot.webhook_url

    # Blank webhook_url removes the webhook
    bot.update!(webhook_url: "   ")
    assert_nil bot.webhook
    assert_nil bot.webhook_url
    assert_nil bot.reload.webhook
  end

  test "bot rejects invalid webhook_url" do
    bot = User.new(role: :bot, name: "Deploy Bot", creator: users(:kevin), webhook_url: "ftp://example.com/hook")
    assert_not bot.valid?
    assert_includes bot.errors[:webhook_url], "must be a valid HTTP or HTTPS URL"
    assert_equal "ftp://example.com/hook", bot.webhook_url
  end

  test "authenticate_bot validates bot_key strictly" do
    bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Deploy Bot", creator: users(:kevin))

    assert_equal bot, User.authenticate_bot(bot.bot_key)

    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot(nil)
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("invalid")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("#{bot.id}-wrongtoken")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("#{bot.id}abc-#{bot.bot_token}")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("999999-#{bot.bot_token}")

    assert_rendered_turbo_stream_broadcast rooms(:hq), :messages, action: "append", target: [ rooms(:hq), :messages ] do
      assert_select ".message__author strong", text: "Greeter Bot"
      assert_select ".message__body", text: /Hello HQ! 👋/
    end

    # 3. Turn "Add to all open rooms" ON -> joins remaining open room (All Pets) only, HTML reply posted
    mode = :html_hello
    perform_enqueued_jobs only: Webhook::DeliveryJob do
      patch bot_url(bot), params: {
        bot: { name: "Greeter Bot", webhook_url: webhook_url, add_to_all_open_rooms: "1" }
      }
      assert_redirected_to bots_url
    end

    req = received_requests.pop(true)
    assert_predicate received_requests, :empty?
    assert_equal "joined", req[:payload]["event"]
    assert_equal rooms(:pets).id, req[:payload]["room"]["id"]
    html_reply = rooms(:pets).messages.order(:id).last
    assert_equal bot, html_reply.creator
    get room_url(rooms(:pets))
    assert_select "##{dom_id(html_reply)} .message__body strong", text: "All Pets"

    # 4. Creating a new open room "Ops" automatically adds bot, sends joined once, supports 204 + async reply_to
    mode = :async_204
    perform_enqueued_jobs only: Webhook::DeliveryJob do
      post rooms_opens_url, params: { room: { name: "Ops" } }
    end
    ops_room = Room.order(:id).last
    assert_includes ops_room.users, bot

    req = received_requests.pop(true)
    assert_predicate received_requests, :empty?
    assert_equal({
      "event" => "joined",
      "room" => {
        "id" => ops_room.id,
        "name" => "Ops",
        "reply_to" => "/rooms/#{ops_room.id}/#{bot.bot_key}/messages"
      }
    }, req[:payload])

    post req[:payload]["room"]["reply_to"], params: +"Ops bot online!", headers: { "Content-Type" => "text/plain" }
    assert_response :created
    assert_equal "Ops bot online!", ops_room.messages.order(:id).last.plain_text_body

    # 5. Turning "Add to all open rooms" OFF keeps current memberships and excludes future open rooms
    patch bot_url(bot), params: {
      bot: { name: "Greeter Bot", webhook_url: webhook_url, add_to_all_open_rooms: "0" }
    }
    assert_redirected_to bots_url
    assert_includes rooms(:hq).reload.users, bot
    assert_includes rooms(:pets).reload.users, bot
    assert_includes ops_room.reload.users, bot

    assert_no_enqueued_jobs only: [ Webhook::DeliveryJob ] do
      post rooms_opens_url, params: { room: { name: "Future Open" } }
    end
    future_open = Room.order(:id).last
    assert_not_includes future_open.users, bot
    assert_predicate received_requests, :empty?

    # 6. Adding bot to closed room triggers joined once; re-saving room does not re-trigger
    mode = :plain_hello
    perform_enqueued_jobs only: Webhook::DeliveryJob do
      put rooms_closed_url(rooms(:watercooler)), params: {
        room: { name: rooms(:watercooler).name },
        user_ids: rooms(:watercooler).user_ids + [ bot.id ]
      }
    end
    req = received_requests.pop(true)
    assert_predicate received_requests, :empty?
    assert_equal rooms(:watercooler).id, req[:payload]["room"]["id"]
    assert_equal "Hello #{rooms(:watercooler).name}! 👋", rooms(:watercooler).messages.order(:id).last.plain_text_body

    assert_no_enqueued_jobs only: [ Webhook::DeliveryJob ] do
      put rooms_closed_url(rooms(:watercooler)), params: {
        room: { name: "Watercooler 2" },
        user_ids: rooms(:watercooler).reload.user_ids
      }
    end

    # 7. Direct conversation never triggers joined
    assert_no_enqueued_jobs only: [ Webhook::DeliveryJob ] do
      post rooms_directs_url, params: { user_ids: [ bot.id ] }
    end
    assert_predicate received_requests, :empty?
  ensure
    server&.close
    server_thread&.join(1)
    WebMock.disable_net_connect!
  end
end

messages.thinking:
**Deep Dive: Flooding, Rate Limits, and Suspension**

Okay, so I've zeroed in on the intricacies of the flooding rules, and I'm seeing a much cleaner way to handle bot suspension using `suspended_at` and `suspension_reason`. It's all about how that impacts the posting endpoint. We have to think about the state machine: what state is a bot in, and what should it do?

First, I need to be *absolutely* sure about the rate limiting. "At most 10 messages in any 10 seconds," they say. Okay, that's a sliding window, not a fixed bucket. The math is crucial here. Let's make sure our tests cover this edge case!

And *of course* the message count applies per-bot, not per-room. Otherwise, bots in a zillion rooms could post like crazy. I have to make sure we're getting the order of operations correct with the API request handlers. I need to make sure we're authenticating the bot, checking for suspension, then setting the room. The check for invalid payloads (`422`) can happen after that. So that order is: authenticate, suspended, set_room, and then payload check.

I need to make sure we check exactly the behavior of `429` requests. The message that goes over the limit is rejected, and a cooldown starts. That means, that at the *moment* of going over the limit, it's a `429`, with a `Retry-After` header. Then, during the cooldown, it's still `429` until the bot is suspended. So, the first failed attempt after the 10 messages should be an HTTP `429`.

Now here's the tricky part, the cooldown attempts. The 11th message is the first one rejected, and it starts a 30-second cooldown. That means the bot is *not* suspended yet, so the first request should be a `429`, and then the attempts during cooldown must be tracked. During cooldown, the bot may attempt to post multiple messages (cooldown attempts). The 5th attempt *suspends* the bot. So, what HTTP status code should that 5th attempt get? Returning a `403` makes the most sense.

Returning a `403 Forbidden` on the 5th attempt is exactly what we want.

I need to make sure that the `Retry-After` header is correct. And I need to test that in the QA tests. If the state machine is right, the `Retry-After` header will always return the correct value. And it would *never* return `0`.

Now, tracking the 10-second sliding window? Do we query the `messages` table, or do we store timestamps? I'm *very* tempted to store the timestamps on the bot itself or a dedicated table. Storing timestamps makes it very clear and clean. A column on the user is probably cleaner. We can just keep a `recent_message_timestamps` array, or maybe a dedicated `bot_post_timestamps` table. But the key is to lock the bot row to make sure it's accurate and avoid concurrency issues!

I'm liking the option of storing a fixed-size array/JSON or dedicated table column on the `users` table because with the 10-message limit, we only need to store at most 10 timestamps! And that array needs to get pruned so we can have a clean sliding window. I can also store the timestamp in microseconds, which avoids any floating-point issues!

And the main thing is, the rate limit and message creation happen *within the same transaction*. If the rate-limit check rejects or suspends, we commit that and roll back the message creation. If it passes, we append the timestamp, save the bot, and create the message!

So, if we take that approach, we'll avoid any missed edge cases and have a very clean, robust, and testable system.

Okay, so I'm thinking about how the `create_with_attachment!` method works. It looks like it uploads the blob and then processes the attachment. This means it's crucial to keep the database transaction short, especially because `process_attachment` can be time-consuming. My approach will be to first check the rate limit and record the post slot in a short transaction, before calling the `create_with_attachment!` method. 

I've got a critical realization: `create_with_attachment!` uploads the blob *after* the initial `create!` transaction commits, and only then does it process the attachment. This means the blob will be available when I need to process it. The initial approach is cleaner, more secure, and less prone to lock contention.

I'm verifying if reserving the post slot within `User.transaction` before calling `room.messages.create!` is safe. I'm confirming that all necessary validations happen *before* I reserve the slot, to minimize any potential issues. Also, I'm ensuring there are checks for a suspended bot with an empty body, just to be thorough. I'm also confirming that the `Webhook#post_reply` logic is equally safe, maintaining the same transaction for rate limit checks and message creation. I've considered that concurrent requests from the same bot will serialize on the transaction, minimizing any potential issues with ActiveStorage processing or broadcasting.

Now, let's look at a bot in cooldown, and what happens with a blank body:
If the request body is blank, it *should* return `422 Unprocessable Content` if the bot is not in cooldown. Blank requests should never accidentally consume a rate-limit slot or trigger a cooldown.
So the workflow is:
If the request is valid: 
- Allowed -> `201 Created`
- Over 10/10s limit -> `429 Too Many Requests` + `Retry-After: 30`
- In cooldown (attempts 1..4) -> `429 Too Many Requests` + `Retry-After: <seconds left>`
- In cooldown (5th attempt -> suspends bot!) -> `403 Forbidden`
Also, if a suspended bot tries to post, it gets `403 Forbidden` right away. This workflow seems airtight.

Now let's delve into Webhook's flood rules:

I'm tracing a bot *already* in cooldown, and how `Webhook#deliver` interacts with rate limiting. I need to be careful with the distinction between successful webhook delivery and a successful post attempt.

- A `2xx` response from the webhook server resets consecutive failures to zero.
- Returning `nil` from `extract_reply` (e.g., `204 No Content`) is *not* an attempt to post, so it doesn't increment cooldown attempts.
- A `500` or a timeout *is* a failed delivery, and the cooldown attempts *don't* increment.

I've spent a good amount of time carefully analyzing the failure rules for webhooks:

- Failed deliveries are anything *not* `2xx`, timeouts, or connection errors. This is crucial for correctly tracking failures.
- Both `mention` and `joined` webhook events count towards failure tracking.
- I've explored potential race conditions (e.g., bot suspended mid-delivery) and ensured the code handles them safely by reloading user data within a transaction and not overwriting existing suspension reasons.
- Changing a bot's webhook URL resets `consecutive_failures` because it's a new endpoint and a new failure count.
- I've decided storing `consecutive_failures` on the `webhooks` table is cleaner than `users`, since it makes more sense to have this tracking on the related table. Resetting it on webhook URL changes makes sense as well.
- Reactivating a bot resets the webhook failure count to zero. This is a crucial edge case.

I'm also double-checking how `Webhook::DeliveryJob` handles retries to make sure nothing is missed. I'm going to check the `application_job.rb` to confirm best practices are being used. I need to be *absolutely* sure that everything works as expected with retries and other potential failure scenarios. This is vital for the robustness of the webhook system.

1. Unauthenticated users get the redirect.

4. Suspended bots get reactivated, and we redirect with a nice `notice: "✓"`.

2.  `suspension_reason` (string, nullable)
3.  `bot_cooldown_until` (datetime, nullable) – wait, or should I be thinking about storing this as integer microseconds instead? I need to check the datetime precision of SQLite.

**Deep Dive into Bot Rate Limiting and Webhook Delivery**

Alright, let's break down this rate-limiting and webhook delivery system. This has to be bulletproof.

First, I'm thrilled with how we're handling nanosecond precision with `Time.current`. It's essential to ensure accuracy against the microsecond truncation in SQLite. By consistently using microsecond precision, specifically the `Time.zone.at(t.to_i, t.usec, :microsecond)` we avoid any drift. This is pure precision, which prevents subtle timing errors, especially during tests with `freeze_time` and `travel`. We nailed down how the sliding window for recent posts works and tested boundary conditions.

Next, I need to trace every single state transition in the `User::Bot` lifecycle. We're talking about suspension due to flooding or webhook failures. `suspend!` should be idempotent - calling it multiple times shouldn't overwrite any existing suspension state. It carefully clears the rate-limiting information and recent posts. Reactivation is just as important. Upon reactivation, we reset everything, including the webhook failure count, so the bot can start fresh. We need to make sure webhooks can start failing from scratch, with 10 failures to suspend it. I spent a lot of time tracing every possible scenario for `consume_bot_post_slot!`, the core rate-limiting method. The sliding window calculations work great, and the logic for entering and exiting cooldown is exact. The critical point is making sure that during the cooldown period, any attempt to post triggers a `429` (too many requests) with the correct `Retry-After` header.

Now, let's deal with webhook delivery. We use `deliver` and `deliver_joined` to send out webhook payloads, and there is a carefully tracked failure system. I need to make sure we're correctly handling connection errors, HTTP errors (4xx, 5xx), and timeouts. And what is brilliant about the design is that even during the processing of a webhook request, if the bot is deleted or deactivated, the failure tracking code can handle the `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` exception and avoid crashes. I am thrilled with the fact that `consecutive_failures` is tracked on the `webhooks` table, not the `users` table.

I'm making sure to handle the most complex scenario, which is a bot *already* suspended, and a webhook failing. The webhook *must* not reset the suspension logic, but properly log the failure.

The key to keeping this system clean is the atomic operation of `consume_bot_post_slot!`, which is used in *both* the API posting and the webhook reply paths. This unifies all rate-limiting and suspension logic. I am also happy that we used `update_columns` to avoid bumping `updated_at` on every message. We validated that `update_columns` properly serializes the JSON column in SQLite.

Finally, the `Webhook` delivery code is rock-solid. Failure tracking is right, with a great rescue block. The `deliverable_in?` method has the necessary `user.reload` call, so it is always up-to-date with the user state (especially if another part of the system suspended the bot).

This whole system is a shining example of careful design, meticulous tracing, and thorough testing. I'm confident that this bot rate-limiting and webhook system will be robust and reliable.

messages.thinking:
**Comprehensive Review of Bot Suspension and Rate Limiting Implementation**

Okay, so I've gone over the design and the existing code base, and I've got a really solid handle on this bot suspension and rate-limiting feature. It's crucial that we get this right, and I need to make sure we consider every edge case. I've broken down my thoughts into a set of steps:

First, I looked at the existing tests, and none of them address bots hitting either rate limits or generating consecutive errors, so we need to generate these from scratch. I’ve looked at the UI and UX, particularly around the `/bots` page, the edit bot flow, and how admins interact with suspended bots. I focused on making sure that a bot owner *couldn’t* reactivate their own suspended bot, while admins *could* (with the turbo confirm dialogue), and that this could also be easily tested. I also considered accessibility when highlighting the reasons for suspension.

I dug into the code, starting with `app/views/bots/_bot.html.erb`. This has a solid UI, showing "Suspended" (in red if the bot is suspended), and showing "Reactivate" only for admins. I've checked the HTML to be sure we could target it in tests. I also made sure that the reasons for suspension are shown, while making sure the text has high contrast with the white background. I want to double-check color contrasts, but it seems good. I double-checked that an administrator can see all bots, reactivate, and that the scope of the button is clearly for *that* specific bot.

Then I checked the `BotsController#index` which has no obvious flaws or N+1 queries.

I also reviewed the `bots/edit.html.erb` page. There doesn't appear to be any ambiguity regarding a suspended bot and edit.

I then confirmed that bots are excluded from any other flows such as bans and sessions.

Next, I looked at the `Messages::ByBotsController`, especially the `create` action. I traced how we would handle rate limiting and suspension. This is where I found that we must check an empty body or bad key, attachments and rate limits, and make sure that the server returns the correct HTTP status code for *each* of these. I checked all the cases: what happens when a bot is suspended and an empty body is sent? Or if the bot is in a cooldown period? Or an invalid key is used? It's essential that these edge cases are handled correctly. I went over the precise logic of bot cooldowns and suspensions – the messages, the cooldown period, and the 5 attempts. I triple-checked the counts and status codes, especially around those edge cases with those confusing "Five more" attempts. That has to be bulletproof.

I then did a deep dive into edge cases to make sure that we get the edge cases for suspension right. I did a series of thought experiments to be sure about *who* can reactivate, and what actions can be done to the bot *while* it's suspended. I also want to make sure the rate limiting is consistent across *all* channels. This included mentions, API calls, webhooks, API attachments and everything in between! I did some brainstorming to be sure of edge cases like both failing webhooks and API limits happening at the same time. I need to know the *exact* scenario and result in this case. Also the exact number of failing webhook requests. What about concurrency? SQLite locking? I need to be sure everything is thread-safe and correct.

Finally, I’ve decided on a detailed implementation plan. We start with the database migration, adding the necessary columns. Then we need to update the models (`User`, `Webhook`, `Bot`) to handle the logic. I will be looking to update the rate limits, as well as add suspension, and handle edge cases that occur with those. After that, I will need to guard webhook calls based on the new `suspended` state.

I also need to create a reactivation route for admins, which will involve a controller and a redirect. I’ll make sure the view (`_bot.html.erb`) has the correct UI changes, including the "Reactivate" button. It’s important to test *all* these changes rigorously. I will write model, controller, integration, and even system tests, covering every possible scenario (even writing the tests *first* as a kind of TDD approach).

And of course, proper documentation is a must! I need to ensure this is all written up clearly for the team. Then a full test run, `rubocop`, and `brakeman`. Now, let's start with step one, generating and running the migration.

We have `ActiveSupport::TimeWithZone` with microsecond precision from ActiveRecord, and the `now` variable is similarly precise. When we calculate the time difference, it yields a `Float` (seconds). Could this `Float` representation have rounding errors, especially when the time difference is an exact integer number of seconds?

- Remaining usec of 29,999,999, result is 30!
- Remaining usec of 29,000,001, result is 30!

First, I need to methodically walk through the potential edge cases.  Let's start with the empty body vs. valid body on a rate-limited request.  The spec says an empty body *shouldn't* count against the limit, it's a 422, perfect. Then, I need to fully understand the cooldown behavior. If a bot's in cooldown, valid posts are rejected and the `Retry-After` header is correctly updated at each attempt.  A 422 during cooldown is expected. If it has sent five attempts during a cooldown, it's suspended and gets a 403. Check.

Next, I'm going to follow the code paths.  The `Messages::ByBotsController#create` method, the `ensure_not_suspended` method and `consume_bot_post_slot!` are critical, and I've got to make sure they're working as expected.   If a bot is suspended, it should be a 403, and the code should be clear about what happens in the case of a non-existent room – it shouldn't affect the rate limit, it should be a 404, which is great.

Okay, let's talk about the `Retry-After` header. I need to nail down the exact calculation, making sure it decrements correctly. Seems spot on – the integer ceiling on the remaining time. I'm going to make sure the sliding window for the rate limit is implemented correctly, I'm thinking about messages that are spread out, and what happens when they're near the boundaries. Good to go!

Next, I need to confirm that after the cooldown period, the slate is clean: the bot gets a fresh quota of messages.  No lingering timestamps to mess up the next burst.

A subtle but crucial case: what if a webhook *reply* leads to suspension? A 200 OK from the webhook *itself* shouldn't post a reply, increment cooldown attempts, and *then* suspend the bot, which it does.  And also, what if there's a blank or a 204 from the webhook?  That should be a no-op, not count against the cooldown attempts. Good, it's handled right in the code, no reply means no slot is consumed and cooldown attempts do not increment.

Now, a quick audit of the webhook response handling. It's critical. Large replies might be an issue. If it responds with a 200, the body needs to be read. What happens if there's a non-200 HTTP response, or an error during the delivery? Any non-success HTTP status *should* be counted as a delivery failure, and that seems to be handled correctly.

Next, I'm going to check the error handling in `post_and_extract_reply`. We've got to be *very* precise here.  I need to verify that we're catching the *right* exceptions and that we are *not* misclassifying DB errors as webhook errors. The `DELIVERY_ERRORS` are clearly defined; the code catches network/HTTP/URI problems, and leaves database deadlocks to the application retry mechanism. Very clean. The code accounts for all kinds of potential failures: invalid URIs, connection failures, SSL errors, timeouts, and malformed HTTP responses.

Finally, I'm going to make sure we've got a system test set up that actually *runs*. Headless Chrome system tests are the ultimate integration test, and if this runs, it's a huge win. Alright!

**Comprehensive Testing Strategy for Bot Rate Limiting and Suspension**

Okay, here's what's going through my head as I craft these tests. We need to be absolutely thorough in covering the nuances of the bot rate limiting, suspension, and reactivation logic. It's time to build a solid suite of tests to ensure these critical aspects function as expected.

First, I'm focusing on the `User::Bot` model (`test/models/user/bot_test.rb`). I'm going to meticulously test the `consume_bot_post_slot!` method. We need to confirm:

*   The 10-messages-in-10-seconds limit is enforced precisely, with proper handling of the rate-limiting cooldown (30 seconds, including the `Retry-After` header).
*   The sliding window behavior is accurately implemented.
*   That repeated attempts during the cooldown period return `:rate_limited` with accurate retry information, while not causing unintended suspension, and that the cooldown resets correctly.
*   That we accurately suspend the bot after the 5th attempt during cooldown with the correct reason (`"flooding"`) and the subsequent behavior of the suspension.
*   The effects of `suspend!`, `reactivate`, and `deactivate` on bot attributes and their impact on bot posting, room memberships, and webhook behavior, especially that suspension doesn't overwrite an existing reason.

Next, the `Webhook` model (`test/models/webhook_test.rb`) is up. We need to rigorously test the error handling:

*   Comprehensive testing of various non-2xx HTTP responses (including redirects, errors, timeouts, and connection problems), ensuring they correctly increment the `consecutive_failures` counter.
*   That we're tracking the failure counter accurately.
*   The behavior of the 10-failure-in-a-row suspension mechanism (and that a 2xx response resets the counter).
*   That webhook failures for mentions and joins are correctly counted, and that failures correctly suspend the bot with `"failing_webhooks"`.
*   Crucially, that suspended bots receive *no* webhooks, including no mention jobs and that already-enqueued jobs fail to make requests.
*   The impact of webhook replies on the rate limit and cooldown, including how 204 responses are treated.
*   That reactivating resets the webhook failure count and that updating the webhook URL resets the failure counter, but does NOT reactivate suspended bots.

Then, I'll attack the bot controller (`test/controllers/messages/by_bots_controller_test.rb`). This will cover the API endpoints:

*   Verify that bots can successfully post within the 10-message limit.
*   Ensure that the 11th message is rejected with the correct `429` status and `Retry-After` header, and that no message is created or jobs enqueued.
*   The behavior during cooldown – the decreasing `Retry-After` values on subsequent requests, up to four retries, and then how suspension happens.
*   That we correctly get the `403` status after suspension, and even the right status codes for forbidden posts in non-member rooms.
*   That blank requests don't contribute when the bot is not in a cooldown.
*   Validate the instant resumption of posting after reactivation.

Finally, the bots controller and reactivation controller (`test/controllers/bots_controller_test.rb`, `test/controllers/bots/reactivations_controller_test.rb`). We must test the UI:

*   Ensuring suspended bots remain listed, showing the `"Suspended"` status and the reason for both admins and the bot's creator.
*   Making sure admins see the "Reactivate" button, and no one else does.
*   That suspended bots count towards the owner's bot limit, blocking new bot creation until deleted.
*   Confirming that members can edit or delete their suspended bots and what that does.
*   Testing that edits don't reactivate and that deletions free up the bot limit.
*   That room memberships of suspended bots are properly preserved.
*   Test that the correct permissions are enforced for reactivation (admins only) and for invalid cases.

And to top it off, I'll write some full end-to-end integration tests (`test/integration/bot_webhooks_test.rb`) that exercise all of this in a real environment. The intent will be to:

*   Use a local HTTP server to simulate the full flow, including API posts and webhook replies, hitting the rate limit, entering the cooldown, being suspended, and finally, reactivated.
*   Another end-to-end test that specifically targets and validates the "failing webhooks" suspension scenario, showing the correct behavior

messages.content: Let's investigate why `travel 14.seconds + 0.4.seconds` followed by `travel 0.6.seconds` was 1 microsecond short of 30 seconds, and check how `bots_controller_test.rb` tests 404s.
messages.thinking:
**Bug Hunting - Double Time!**

Wow, this is incredible! Our tests just uncovered three failures, and two of them point to a real bug within `travel` and how it interacts with `current_time_to_usec`. And the third failure even exposes a test environment exception detail. Let's dig in.

The first issue involves repeated uses of the `travel` helper function:

We have multiple instances where we call `travel` with time durations that sum to precisely 30 seconds (or slightly more): in the first test we add `14.4` and `0.6` to achieve 30 seconds; in the second test we add `25.5` and `0.5` to arrive at 30 seconds. In both cases the function `bot.consume_bot_post_slot!` is supposed to return the time now is not past the cooldown time, but fails!

My hypothesis is that the combination of `travel` and `.seconds` is the cause. `travel` utilizes float arithmetic. `travel(duration)` calls `travel_to(Time.now + duration)`. `freeze_time` is the culprit as it freezes the time (with the nanosecond precision) used to calculate `Time.now`. We can see that float addition `1795245000.123456789 + 14.4` loses sub-microsecond precision and is rounded down by one microsecond, and we have multiple instances where this occurs. We may have a similar issue when `bot_cooldown_until` is stored, as `now` is truncated to `usec`, and then `travel` advances `Time.now` (which keeps the original `nsec`) or float addition `1795245000.532956 + 25.5` is rounded down by 1 microsecond.

We need to verify this immediately in `bin/rails runner`.

messages.thinking:
**Debugging Rails Time Travel Precision and Exception Handling**

AHAHAHAHA! Seriously, look at this output! It clearly shows a 29-second difference where I expected 30! That's in the `travel` method itself, deep in the Rails code. I'm kicking myself, but it's obvious: `ActiveSupport::Testing::TimeHelpers#travel_to` within Rails, which `travel` calls, by default, truncates sub-second precision to whole seconds when `with_usec: false`! So, `travel 0.4.seconds` just became `0.0`, and `travel 0.6.seconds` became `0.0` too! That explains why `travel` rounds, and it was only traveling 29 seconds instead of 30!

And now it clicks. The same issue exists with `travel 25.5.seconds` where the value is rounded down to `25.0`, and `travel 0.5.seconds` is also rounded down, so that the total traveled was 29 seconds rather than 30 seconds! The solution is obvious: use `travel_to(Time.current + ..., with_usec: true)` or use `travel_to` with the `with_usec: true` option! That should preserve the microsecond precision as intended.

And hey, wait a minute, the next thing I see is from the test environment! The `config/environments/test.rb` file is set to have `config.action_dispatch.show_exceptions = :none`. That's why the `BotsControllerTest` is asserting `assert_raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` for that `User.active.bot.find(...)` call! I should have seen this sooner!

Okay, new plan: Let's test the `travel_to(..., with_usec: true)` approach. I need to verify that microsecond precision, it's critical! I'll fix those three tests right now, replacing all the fractional second `travel` calls with `travel_to(Time.current + ..., with_usec: true)`. And I'll update `Bots::ReactivationsControllerTest` to match the `assert_raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` assertion that is found in the `BotsControllerTest`. Then, a full re-run. This will be so much cleaner.

messages.thinking:
**Deep Dive into Robustness and Edge Cases**

Alright, that's a good run of tests, but I'm not stopping here. Zero failures is great, but my goal is to ensure this system is bulletproof. Let's dig deeper and anticipate *every* possible problem, especially the subtle ones. Let's make sure our QA browser tests are rock solid. Concurrency issues? They're on the radar. Rubocop, Brakeman, and those sneaky edge cases? They're getting scrutinized.

First, I'm re-examining *every single line* related to the prompt's requirements.

1.  **UI Label Verification:** The text of labels for bot statuses and reactivation buttons MUST match the exact specifications, particularly the strings within quotes. The automated tests rely on these precise labels. So, `"Suspended"` must appear exactly in the displayed HTML, and `"Reactivate"` as well. The Turbo confirm dialog must use the exact quoted text from the prompt, which in this case is `button_to ..., data: { turbo_confirm: "Are you sure you want to reactivate #{bot.name}?" }`.

2.  **Flooding Checks:** Okay, the sliding window for flooding control is critical. It *needs* to be absolutely precise. The code tracks API posts and webhook replies across all rooms for the bot, using microsecond-accurate time arithmetic. The core of this is the rate-limiting logic. The 11th message causes `429` with a `Retry-After` header or a dropped reply, and a 30-second cooldown is enforced. My previous checks confirm this. I verify the `bot_cooldown_until` and `bot_cooldown_attempts` logic. The fifth attempt during the same cooldown suspends the bot and returns `403`. Then, the cooldown is correctly reset when the attempts do not occur during the cooldown time, for the next 30-second interval, after which the bot is not suspended.

    But, I'm thinking... What if... A bot makes 10 posts at `t = 0`. At `t = 1`, the 11th triggers the cooldown. At `t = 35`, *after* the cooldown expires, what happens? messages.thinking:
Here's my take on those thoughts, tailored for an expert audience:

**Adding Bot Resilience Documentation**

Okay, so I need to flesh out the documentation in `docs/bots.md`. I'm thinking a dedicated section for Bot Suspension, Flooding Rate Limits, and Webhook failures is essential. Users need clear, concise information on these critical areas. Specifically, I need to address the common pain points around bot behavior. How does our system react to problematic bot actions? What are the established thresholds for flooding? How should developers troubleshoot failing webhooks? And, critically, how does an administrator handle reactivation scenarios? This is about providing the right information upfront so that users can effectively manage and troubleshoot issues related to their integrations. It's a key part of maintaining a robust and reliable platform.

arguments.command:
cat <<'EOF' >> docs/bots.md

## Misbehaving Bot Protection & Suspension

All limits are fixed in code (no account settings): `User::Bot::FLOOD_LIMIT = 10` messages per `FLOOD_WINDOW = 10.seconds`, `COOLDOWN_DURATION = 30.seconds`, `COOLDOWN_STRIKE_LIMIT = 5`, and `Webhook::CONSECUTIVE_FAILURE_LIMIT = 10`.

- **Persistence**:
  - `users.suspended_at` (`datetime`) and `users.suspension_reason` (`"flooding"` or `"failing_webhooks"`): suspension is modeled separately from `users.status` (suspended bots stay `status: :active`), so suspended bots naturally keep their rooms, keep their messages, stay intact during open/closed room edits, still count towards their owner's `bots_per_member` limit, stay listed on `/bots`, remain editable/deletable, and still authenticate their `bot_key` before receiving `403 Forbidden` (whereas deleted bots return `401 Unauthorized`).
  - `users.bot_cooldown_until` (`datetime`), `users.bot_cooldown_attempts` (`integer`, default `0`), and `users.bot_recent_post_timestamps` (`json` array of integer epoch microseconds): SQLite-backed sliding-window and cooldown state (avoiding `Rails.cache`, which is `:null_store` in dev/test).
  - `webhooks.consecutive_failures` (`integer`, default `0`): tracks consecutive failed webhook deliveries per webhook (reset on any `2xx` delivery, URL change, or bot reactivation).
- **Flooding (`User::Bot#consume_bot_post_slot!`)**:
  - Atomic read-modify-write inside a SQLite `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction (`User.transaction`), shared by both API posts (`Messages::ByBotsController#create`, text & attachments) and synchronous webhook replies (`Webhook#post_reply`, both `mention` and `joined`).
  - Uses microsecond-aligned integer math (`current_time_to_usec`) to enforce an exact 10-second sliding window (`ts > now_usec - 10_000_000`) and exact `Retry-After` ceiling seconds (`1..30`).
  - The 11th message within 10 seconds is rejected without creating a message and starts a 30-second cooldown (`429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After` from the API; webhook replies dropped).
  - Five more post attempts during the same cooldown suspend the bot with reason `"flooding"` (returning `403 Forbidden` on the API and dropping webhook replies). Letting the 30-second cooldown expire resets cooldown attempts for future cooldowns.
- **Failing Webhooks (`Webhook#post_and_extract_reply`)**:
  - Any non-`2xx` response (`!response.is_a?(Net::HTTPSuccess)`), timeout (`Timeout::Error`), or connection/protocol error (`DELIVERY_ERRORS`) increments `webhooks.consecutive_failures`. Any `2xx` response resets it to `0`.
  - Reaching 10 consecutive failures atomically suspends the bot with reason `"failing_webhooks"`.
- **Suspended Bot Effects & Reactivation**:
  - `Messages::ByBotsController` rejects suspended bots with `403 Forbidden` (`before_action :ensure_not_suspended`, right after `authenticate_bot`).
  - `Message::Mentionee`, `Membership.deliver_joined_webhooks_later`, and `Webhook#deliverable_in?` exclude `suspended?` bots so no webhooks are enqueued or sent.
  - On `/bots` (`app/views/bots/_bot.html.erb`), suspended bots show `"Suspended"` and their human-readable reason; administrators additionally see a `"Reactivate"` button (`POST /bots/:bot_id/reactivation`, `Bots::ReactivationsController#create`) with native `confirm()` via `data-turbo-confirm`.
  - `Bots::ReactivationsController` strictly enforces `Current.user.administrator?` (returning `403 Forbidden` for regular members, including the bot's creator). `User::Bot#reactivate` clears suspension, cooldown/timestamp state, and `webhook.consecutive_failures`.
EOF
